CALIFORNIA BOT DISCLOSURE LAW (BUS. & PROF. CODE §§ 17940-17943) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee on behalf of Acme, Inc., states what California's Business and Professions Code §§ 17940–17943 provide about disclosing that an online communication or interaction is generated by a bot rather than a person. These sections were added to the Business and Professions Code as Chapter 6, captioned "Bots," by Senate Bill 1001 (2018); the statute's own text does not assign the chapter any other short title, though it is sometimes referred to informally, outside the statute itself, as the "B.O.T. Act" or "Bolstering Online Transparency Act." This sheet states what that chapter's own text says; it does not evaluate whether any particular account, message, or business practice complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "BOT," "ONLINE," AND "PERSON"
Business and Professions Code § 17940 defines the terms used throughout this chapter. A "bot" means an automated online account where all or substantially all of the actions or posts of that account are not the result of a person — that is, the statute defines the term by reference to an account's degree of automation, not by reference to any particular software architecture or technology. "Online" means appearing on any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication. "Person," for purposes of this chapter, is defined broadly to include not only a natural person but also a corporation, limited liability company, partnership, joint venture, association, estate, trust, government, governmental subdivision or agency, or other legal entity, or any combination of those.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Bot” means an automated online account where all or substantially all of the actions or posts of that account are not the result of a person."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(a), Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17940.)
  "“Online” means appearing on any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(b), Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17940.)
  "“Person” means a natural person, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, joint venture, association, estate, trust, government, governmental subdivision or agency, or other legal entity or any combination thereof."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(d), Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17940.)
  Known gap: These three definitions are drawn from subsections (a), (b), and (d) of the same statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940, and are not independent of one another or of the separate "online platform" definition in that same section's subsection (c), which is quoted in a separate clause below because it is used only in the service-provider exemption at § 17942(c), not in the definitions of "bot," "online," or "person" themselves. This sheet does not address how these definitions apply to any specific automated account, technology, or business, and it does not address whether any particular account is or is not "substantially" automated within the meaning of the "bot" definition.

THE CORE PROHIBITION: BOT USE WITH INTENT TO MISLEAD ABOUT ARTIFICIAL IDENTITY
Business and Professions Code § 17941(a) makes it unlawful for any person to use a bot to communicate or interact with another person in California online, with the intent to mislead the other person about its artificial identity, for the purpose of knowingly deceiving the person about the content of the communication, in order to incentivize a purchase or sale of goods or services in a commercial transaction or to influence a vote in an election. The statute frames this as two layered mental-state elements — an intent to mislead about the bot's artificial identity, coupled with a purpose of knowingly deceiving about the content of the communication — directed at one of two specific ends: a commercial purchase-or-sale transaction, or an election vote. It is not, by its own terms, a general prohibition on all undisclosed bot activity online. The same subsection also states that a person using a bot is not liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) It shall be unlawful for any person to use a bot to communicate or interact with another person in California online, with the intent to mislead the other person about its artificial identity for the purpose of knowingly deceiving the person about the content of the communication in order to incentivize a purchase or sale of goods or services in a commercial transaction or to influence a vote in an election. A person using a bot shall not be liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17941(a), Bots (Chapter 6), Unlawful Use of an Undisclosed Bot (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17941.)
  Known gap: This clause states only what § 17941(a) itself says about the prohibition and its disclosure-based exception; it does not state what counts as an adequate disclosure, which is addressed by § 17941(b) in a separate clause below — subsections (a) and (b) are part of the same statutory section and are not independent sources of authority from one another. This sheet does not address how the "intent to mislead" or "knowingly deceiving" elements would be proven or evaluated in any particular case, does not restate § 17942(a)'s statement that the chapter's duties are cumulative with other law, and does not address whether any particular automated account or communication falls within the prohibition.

WHAT THE STATUTE REQUIRES OF AN ADEQUATE DISCLOSURE
Business and Professions Code § 17941(b) states the standard for the disclosure that removes liability under subsection (a): the disclosure must be clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed to inform persons with whom the bot communicates or interacts that it is a bot. The statute states this standard in general terms; its own text does not further define "clear," "conspicuous," or "reasonably designed," does not specify any particular wording, placement, format, or timing for the disclosure, and does not describe any specific disclosure method as automatically sufficient.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) The disclosure required by this section shall be clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed to inform persons with whom the bot communicates or interacts that it is a bot."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17941(b), Bots (Chapter 6), Disclosure Standard (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17941.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the general standard in § 17941(b)'s own text. This chapter does not itself define what disclosure content or format satisfies "clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed"; this sheet does not identify any implementing regulations, administrative guidance, or case law construing that standard, and this research did not locate a codified safe harbor in this chapter. Subsection (b) is part of the same statutory section as the core prohibition in subsection (a), addressed in a separate clause above, and the two are not independent sources of authority from one another.

EXEMPTION FOR SERVICE PROVIDERS OF ONLINE PLATFORMS
Business and Professions Code § 17942(c) states that this chapter does not impose a duty on service providers of online platforms, including, but not limited to, web hosting and Internet service providers. The chapter separately defines "online platform," in § 17940(c), as any public-facing Internet website, web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication, that has 10,000,000 or more unique monthly United States visitors or users for a majority of months during the preceding 12 months.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Online platform” means any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication, that has 10,000,000 or more unique monthly United States visitors or users for a majority of months during the preceding 12 months."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(c), Bots (Chapter 6), "Online Platform" Defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17940.)
  "(c) This chapter does not impose a duty on service providers of online platforms, including, but not limited to, Web hosting and Internet service providers."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17942(c), Bots (Chapter 6), Service Provider Exemption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=17942.)
  Known gap: Because "online platform" is a defined term carrying the 10,000,000-monthly-visitor threshold quoted above, § 17942(c)'s exemption for service providers of "online platforms," read together with that definition, is narrower than an exemption for service providers of any website or app regardless of size — this sheet does not resolve whether or how that threshold would be applied to a given service provider or platform. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17940 and 17942 are two separate, independently numbered sections; the two citations below are independent of one another. This sheet does not otherwise address what "service providers" of an online platform means, and this research did not locate any other exemption stated in this chapter's own text besides this one.

CERTIFICATION
I, Jordan Lee, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17940–17943, for informational reference only regarding Acme, Inc. This information sheet does not evaluate whether any particular account, communication, or practice of Acme, Inc. complies with this chapter, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Executed on September 5, 2026.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________
